query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace amounts (<1 at.%) of Hf to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will precipitate nanoscale Hf-rich phases along the interlamellar boundaries, thereby pinning these interfaces to suppress microcrack initiation and propagation, which in turn will simultaneously improve both the alloy's yield/tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a dual-phase lamellar (e.g., FCC/B2) microstructure with numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce trace Hf additions (<1 at.%) into the alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing and standard thermo-mechanical processing (casting, rolling, annealing) that yields the dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates forming at the interlamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The trace Hf additions will form nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates that act as pins at the internal boundaries. This pinning reduces boundary sliding and microcrack initiation while concurrently providing precipitation strengthening. The combined effect is expected to enhance load transfer across phases, thereby improving both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Hf-modified alloy is expected to exhibit a statistically significant increase in both yield/ultimate tensile strength and tensile ductility relative to the baseline unmodified eutectic HEA.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic HEA with its conventional lamellar colony structure and inherent susceptibility to room-temperature microcracking.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only within a narrow Hf addition range (trace levels, ideally <1 at.%). Excessive Hf may lead to the formation of overly coarse or brittle intermetallic phases, which could counteract the intended improvements.
generation.uncertainty: While precipitation strengthening and boundary-pinning effects observed at high temperatures suggest promise, the exact optimal Hf concentration for room-temperature performance and the precise magnitude of the improvements are not yet well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of eutectic HEA samples using identical processing routes, one group with trace (<1 at.%) Hf additions and one group without Hf. Ensure both groups develop a similar lamellar colony microstructure. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and conduct microstructural characterization using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and total tensile strain
Presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates at interlamellar boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the expected Hf-rich precipitates at the internal boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.

Multiphase alloys with heterogeneous microstructures demonstrate excellent combination of strength and ductility, making them attractive for myriad structural applications [,,]. Recently, eutectic high entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple solid solution phases have been the subject of extensive research due to their promise of overcoming the strength-ductility tradeoff seen in metals and conventional alloys [,,,,,,,]. The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy represents a canonical example of an eutectic HEA with the lamellar arrangement of CoCrFe-rich L12 and AlNi-rich B2 phases [], which exhibit an excellent combination of strength and ductility at room temperature as well as exceptional strain hardening behavior that is largely retained up to 700 °C. Different processing routes have been utilized for achieving a wide range of microstructural features, resulting in outstanding mechanical properties and excellent corrosion resistance in these alloys. The ease of attaining ultrafine microstructure in directly cast eutectic HEAs is uncommon in conventional alloys []. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

reading.lever: Introduce trace Hf additions to the eutectic HEA to precipitate nanoscale Hf-rich phases at interlamellar boundaries.
reading.why: This approach leverages proven precipitation and boundary‐pinning effects in similar HEAs to mitigate microcrack initiation while enhancing strength and ductility at room temperature.
